title: At the pharmacy
setting: A small pharmacy (apotek) on a busy street in Yogyakarta. You've had an upset stomach since last night. A young woman in a white coat is behind the counter.

n1.speaker: pharmacist
n1.indonesian: Sore, Kak. Ada yang bisa dibantu?

options.indonesian: Saya sakit perut, Mbak. Sejak tadi malam.
options.english: I've got an upset stomach, since last night.
options.feedback: Specific and clear: what's wrong, and since when. Mbak suits a young woman behind a counter.
True, but vague: she needs to know what kind of sick. Name it, as in Saya sakit perut (I've got a stomach ache).
English 'have' carried over. You don't 'have' an ache with punya: say Saya sakit perut, or Perut saya sakit.

n2.speaker: pharmacist
n2.indonesian: Sakit apa, Kak? Sakitnya di mana?
n2.english: What's the trouble? Where does it hurt?

options.feedback: Pointing to the spot works anywhere, and she'll give you the word for it.
Perut saya sakit (my stomach hurts) means the same as saya sakit perut.

n3.speaker: pharmacist
n3.english: A stomach ache, then. Diarrhoea too?

options.feedback: Saying how often helps her choose the right medicine. Kali is 'times'.
Hanya (only, just) narrows it down for her.

n4.speaker: pharmacist
n4.english: Are you allergic to any medicines?

options.feedback: Tidak ada (there isn't any) is the natural answer to an Ada …? question.
Always worth saying. For a serious allergy, have it written on your phone too.
Bukan denies a noun: it's not that thing. To say you don't have any, it's tidak ada.

n5.speaker: pharmacist
n5.indonesian: Ini obatnya, Kak. Diminum tiga kali sehari, satu tablet, sesudah makan. Banyak minum air putih juga, ya.
n5.english: Here's the medicine. One tablet three times a day, after meals. And drink plenty of water.

options.indonesian: Tiga kali sehari, sesudah makan. Baik, Mbak.
options.english: Three times a day, after meals. OK.
options.feedback: Repeating the dose back is the surest way to get it right.
She said sesudah makan: after meals. Sebelum is before, the opposite.

options.indonesian: Saya ambil obat ini tiga kali sehari, ya?
options.english: I take this medicine three times a day?
options.feedback: Ambil is to take as in pick up or fetch. In Indonesian you drink medicine, even tablets: minum obat.

n6.speaker: pharmacist
n6.indonesian: Semuanya tiga puluh lima ribu, Kak.

options.feedback: Handing over the exact amount saves everyone hunting for change.
Pharmacy chains usually take cards; a small one may be cash only, so ask first.
She said tiga puluh lima ribu: thirty-five thousand. Puluh is tens and ratus is hundreds.

n7.speaker: pharmacist
n7.indonesian: Terima kasih. Semoga cepat sembuh, Kak.
n7.english: Thank you. I hope you feel better soon.

options.feedback: Amin is the usual answer to a wish that starts with semoga (may it be that), whatever your faith.
Simple and right for a kind wish.

end.speaker: narration
end.english: Sorted. An apotek sells many medicines over the counter, and the staff expect you to describe the problem: sakit perut, diare or demam, and since when. In Indonesian you drink medicine (minum obat), and the dose comes as tiga kali sehari, sesudah makan. If you're no better in a couple of days, see a doctor.
